entry.title: A love letter to mymind
entry.content:
.. and a case for entropy

What are some digital rituals you participate in?

– Prompt from Bangalore IndieWebClub meetup #33.

I have loved links for as long as I can remember. Links to blogs, to videos, to images, to apps, to papers, to obscure ideas on the other side of the planet. Another thing I have loved nearly as much is collecting curating them and sharing them with friends and family, even though I know they do not check out most of them (sigh).

Sharing is one part of the appeal. More importantly, I love coming back to the links I have saved. Each one feels like an old entry in my diary, a recollection of something I cared about enough to save it. Over time, the collection becomes a record of my attention. A journal, or a trail of what I found worth keeping.

A graveyard of failed attempts

In my love of links also lies a problem. It usually begins when a critical quantity of links have been saved, and now they need to be organised into a searchable archive. This is where things start going downhill.

I have tried dozens of “second brain” tools and paid obnoxious amounts in subscription fees over the years to satiate this obsession with links. Most of these tools make the same promises: put everything here, organise it well, and you will always be able to return to your ideas for perpetuity.

The tricky part being “organise it well”.

All of these tools demand that you maintain a structure, one they have decided is the best way to build your system. It usually involves some combination of folders, tags, databases, links, naming conventions, and rules about where things belong. Commit to the vocabulary of the application, and you will succeed!

You decide to take the leap and commit to a structure, one that mostly makes sense when you create it. But as you collect more links, explore newer corners and vast depths of the web, the way you categorise these links and your own ideas keeps evolving.

A category that felt obvious six months ago starts feeling arbitrary. Two interests that once seemed separate turn out to be connected. Some links matter before there is a language for why they matter, and then every characteristic about it is being manually labelled and categorised every time.

Eventually, maintaining the system becomes the task, and saving and exploring links loses its meaning.

Perhaps some amount of entropy is not a failure of the system. It is simply a reflection of how our interests grow and evolve.

A place for almost anything

As I was walking the halls of despair, dejected by my failure to organise my beloved links, I came across mymind. Another app that promises to solve all the problems I have been complaining about.

“Remember everything. Organize nothing.” read their tagline. What a concept!

I was cynical at first, but I am also addicted to the idea of completely uprooting and porting my digital presence every three months. So I gave it a shot.

Soon enough, I was saving everything I wanted to preserve and remember in the app: articles, images, notes, repositories, music, books, products, and things I did not even know could be saved. Finding them again was painless too. I could type a keyword, an idea, or even a visual characteristic, and the app would surface related links for me.

That was more than three years ago. Now, more than 1,800 items later, I cannot imagine my life without mymind.

At this point, I should probably disclose that this is not an advertisement for the app, even though I absolutely love it and could not be convinced otherwise.

A place like my actual mind?

In mymind, my thoughts do not live in neat folders. They move more like objects flowing in a river. I notice one, pick it up, examine it, connect it to something else, and then drop it back into the current. I may return to it later in a different context.

mymind feels closer to my actual mind than most second-brain tools ever have.

There is no rigid system asking me to decide what something is or where it belongs at the moment I save it. It is a forgiving system that lets me collect ideas freely and return to them when I please.

Probably my favourite feature of the app is Serendipity, a tab where the app resurfaces old links at random, presenting you with the opportunity to keep or forget each one.

There are so many features I have not even talked about here. I highly recommend checking out mymind for yourself.

A dream for software

My experience with mymind also points to a larger belief I hold about software.

At the risk of borrowing from Marie Kondo, software should spark joy when you use it. Software should adapt to the way the user thinks and works. It should help you do something you care about without constantly reminding you, or more accurately, shouting from the rooftops, about its own infrastructure and systems.

Too much software forces people to adapt to arbitrary choices shaped by the priorities of the system. You must use its categories, follow its workflow, and maintain the structure it expects. The burden of compatibility falls on you.

Entropy is inevitable in any system that grows with a person. The challenge for software is not to eliminate it, but to absorb it without passing the burden back to the user.

The best software makes you forget that this infrastructure exists at all. It becomes invisible because it adapts to how you want to work. It can lead when you need direction, follow when you know where you are going, and move alongside you as your habits and interests evolve.

As mymind becomes a more integral part of my life, I also realise that I have barely scratched the surface of what it can be for me. There are still so many ways to return to the things I have saved, find old ideas in new contexts, and discover connections I did not know were there. More than three years in, I am still learning how to use it, and look forward to the next turn in this journey.

entry.title: Hesitation to speak up
entry.content:
So this is my entry to a prompt "How does an idea qualify to be a post on your website?" I received at an IndieWeb Meetup.

It is a peculiar thing for me, isn't it? If you've tried to read more of my blog posts, you'll quickly realise how I don't even have a setup to paginate my blog posts. Yet, as I write this post, I can see I already have 7 drafts that haven't yet "qualified" to be part of my website.

Why? When I read some of those, I see great value, funny anecdotes, and something that I do cherish and feel cutely expresses my thoughts of the past. Yet I still feel something is still missing. Maybe they are too unstructured, maybe they are too blunt, maybe they are too personal, or maybe I want to say more, but I am not there yet.

Before I investigate further, I should acknowledge that procrastination is a major factor here. The fact that almost all of my recent blog posts are "my entry to a prompt at IndieWeb" tells me that I really need to be put in a spot to cough up something. In fact, I joined IndieWeb solely because I doubted anyone was remotely interested in reading anything I had to say. That internal critic prevented so many of my thoughts from even reaching the draft stage.

Say, I got over that critic, or an idea was just so loud that I just had to type the thoughts with whatever limited vocabulary I had access to, why would I hesitate to publish it? Is it just about how messy the thoughts are?

Say, I even polished it up, why do I still not publish it? How come I have a very polished draft from 2017 that is still unpublished? And how come I published every post when prompted at IndieWeb? What's the difference? Certainly it is not about polish either.

🔗intention

I think, ultimately, incoherent or not, I hesitate to take space, even if digitally. I procrastinate, I fear immense judgment or worse, indifference, and keep my thoughts to myself.

But the act of being in a community (IndieWeb), hearing so many wonderful people typing away their beautiful thoughts, and even reading mine and liking, nay, loving it makes me feel secure. This is more about my outlook of myself in the world, and less about the quality of my writing. My procrastination is a symptom of my hesitation, not the other way round.

🔗read the question again

The prompt wasn't about how I allow myself to take space, but about how an idea qualifies to be a post. I have lots of ideas, I even write about some, and at times post them on my website. Which ideas qualify?

This requires me to answer the question "what purpose does my website serve". Right now, in my unsure 30s, it is about self-discovery and self-expression. The more authentic it is, the more worthwhile it is to me, the more qualified it becomes. Sadly, this requires me to discover myself more, express myself more, be more sure about my un-surety. And the sure-shot way of accessing that is an interesting prompt that really makes me think, a time constraint and a room full of amazing people willing to listen.

If I could somehow recreate that internally and perpetually, who knows, maybe I too would be able to one-shot my blog posts? Until then, see you at IndieWeb.

🔗one more thing

One of my recent post was actually a draft for years, which in turn was a reflection on my other post from a decade ago. Goes to show how much is left unsaid for how long!

entry.title: On Drafting
What will make me take LinkedIn seriously
entry.content:
You know how LinkedIn shows where we work and what our position there is below our names on every post we make? What it should show instead:

  • Whose stock we own
  • Who has contracted our company’s work, and
  • Whose activities we fund

All in order of their magnitudes and time periods. Only then can I consider taking your enthusiasm for a job, project, or organization and its apparent success seriously.

Since data personalization is so good for the world, let’s go three steps further:

  1. If you post about a company or organization, or things related to it contractually, LinkedIn displays if you own that particular stock or related stocks, and if you’re a contractor or prime for them.
  2. Algorithmically display such posts in order of their potential to move money
  3. Discard likes and reactions from employees on posts made by their company. If anything, internally count them as negative points for an anti-algorithm.

entry.title: Loading Indian Maps on a Garmin Forerunner 965
entry.content:
The primary reason I bought this watch was the ability to display and navigate using proper offline maps. Garmin doesn’t have maps for India. But the OpenStreetMaps community has maps that can be loaded into Garmin. There are many community-built web services, such as Thukke’s OSM Downloads and Userbeam, that provide Indian maps for use on Garmin devices, including routing. I used one by run by BBBike. It creates a map of the area you choose from PlanetOSM‘s extracts and delivers it in the format you want.

Download

  1. Go to BBBikes Garmin Page
  2. Choose the format Garmin OSM (UTF-8). All modern Garmin devices can use UTF-8.
  3. Select the area you want (bbox)
  4. Click on Extract
  5. Once it’s ready, you will get an email.
  6. You can also check the progress on the status page and download it from there.
  7. Extract the zip file to get .img file

Load

  1. Plug into Ubuntu with USB; it should appear as mass storage.
  2. It’s in the Garmin Connect App; On the top right, click on the watch. Go to System > USB Mode; set it to Media Transfer (MTP). Reattach and check.
  3. In my case (Forerunner 965), I had to block the `garmin_gps` kernel module from loading. You can try that too.
  4. Once that is done. Once you connect, the watch will ask for your permission to connect as mass storage
  5. Say yes
  6. It should appear as mass storage
  7. Go to /Garmin/
  8. Paste the downloaded .img file
  9. Safely unmount the Garmin
  10. Now go to the watch and go to Maps Manager
  11. Your map file should be there
  12. Open it and see

entry.title: Publishing a draft "Weight gain to 75kg"
entry.content:
75KG GOAL!

My current weight fluctuates around 61kg to 63kg. This is the case for as far as I can remember. Last year, I check my BMI(Body-Mass index). It's suppose to tell you your ideal weight based on your height and age. I don't know who invented this formula or how it works, but It've been told this is what you should use to find out what your ideal weight should be. So, I added my height, 5.75 ft, and age,30yrs, and my ideal wight came out to be 75kg. now, I fall 10kg to 12kg short of this and it looks on me.For all of my adult life I've been a skinny guy, and I can't tell you for sure, It's not like I've substantial proof for it, but people treat you differently, poorly, when you don't have meat on your bones. Most of the time your unseen or ignored, at rare cases bullied on the streets of Delhi if you're walking alone in a rough neighbourhood, joke at your expense comes easily, and your shoulder becomes an excellent place for people who have more calories then you to rest their arm. now, as I said earlier, I don't have any proof for this, maybe it’s my meek personality , but I've not seen this happen to a 6ft guy with a meek personality. I personally have no qualms with being skinny, on the contrary I like it. I'm no foodie, so less time spent eating, and shitting, works fine for me. But, as we are judged and treated differently based on our appearance, I want to see what holds on the other side for me.

So , now that I've explained my motivation. I would like to present you my plan.

1kg of weight equals to 7,700 calories. Let's say I need to gain 12kgs to reach my 75kg weight goal. So, that's a total of 92,400 calories.

I need to eat this many calories on top of my current meals. Let me explain what my daily diet looks like. breakfast:Idli or rava idli or upma, or 2 eggs coffee/tea Lunch: 2 roti, 1 dal, 1 sabzi coffee/tea sometimes fruitbowl dinner: 2 roti, 1 dal, 1 sabzi, 2 spoon rice. this is 1000 to 1300 calories.

Since my weight hasn't increased that means I've achieved (better to say my body ) equilibrium, most if not all of my calories are burn to sustain me. I think hardly any fat is stored but, I'm seeing belly fat so maybe I'm wrong.

now, if I was in a fantasy world or scifi future, I would simply take this many calories, shove it down my throat, and gain weight, but unfortunately we are in a universe with a lot of rules to be followed. So, I've to do this in the long, hard, and boring way.

The food we eat has to be broken down and absorbed. This is where our digestive system comes in. We all have different stomach sizes but a human stomach can safely contain up to 1 liter. Then the food has to passed through the digestive tract. There are limits to how much and how fast the stomach can absorb food, for example, it can absorb 50-60 grams of calories in an hour.

Considering everything there's a theoretical limit of 4000 calories a day. now, I simply can't go from 1000 ish calories to 4000 calories as my stomach and mind is only used to small portion sizes. After every meal, a hormone is release that gives that fulfilling happy sensation of satisfaction. (sidenote: The Ozampic is made out of this), so I'll never be able to intake so many calories. The way to eat more is to trick the stomach into eating more calories. Unsurprisingly liquids trick the stomach into eating more calories and don't trigger that fullness hormones. Also, I'll have to up the daily, small portion size, meals from 3 to 5. To keep my digestive system running like an amazon warehouse factory or an AI datacenter.

Now, if i double my calorie intake to 2200cal a day, I've figured out how, then I should be able to reach my goal of 92,400cal in (92,400 divide by 1100 surplus claries) 84 days that's almost 3 months. (sidenote: I won't get 100% calorie absorption since fiber rich food take more energy to absorb and there's guy batteries that take some of the calories for themselves.)

now, all I've to do is figure out from which food to get those 1100 calories and how to avoid my body storing those calories as fat around my tummy.

entry.title: week notes May to June something 2026 san francisco san jose california ((part one??))
entry.content:
The tall dutch airhost saw my ticket. San Francisco?! Oh my god. I'm sorry for you. Your seat's that way.

I sat there for some time. The plane landed at Schiphol. I walked out of the exit door and through the aerobridge, and found myself at the gate for the next flight. A middle aged Goan started chatting with me. Works at the ship, he said. He was flirting with me, a fact I didn't pick up on until he mentioned that we "do something" in the bathroom. I politely declined.

I walked through the boarding gate, which took me to a Mediterranean fast food place in a shady part of SoMa. I was with my colleague, and I saw my brother walk in. It occurred to me that I hadn't seen him in a long time. He only wanted soup. There was shouting outside.

We walked out. It's too shady here, my brother said. Let's book cabs. Our Lyft arrived. When I got inside it was suddenly daytime. The bearded driver jovially asked us to say Hi to Chewbacca. I looked back to see a random fuzzy monkey-esque soft toy, and I chuckled. I'm having the best day ever, he said. Glad to catch you in this mood, I said. Yeah I broke up with my girlfriend. He spoke about how his daughter (how stupid is she) working at the bar is secretly an alcoholic, but she won't admit it.

I had to awkwardly end the conversation as I deboarded. This was at an San Jose dinner party. I saw an old close friend (who I lost touch with for a bit) win an award for his conference paper just as I entered the restaurant courtyard. A waiter walking around showed me a tray with a drink and I took it. I realised I didn't want one. Over the barbeque flames, the head of AI at a popular database company talked about how much he hated that shit. And then made a job offer to my old friend's friend sitting beside me. It was cold. I stared at the fire.

I went back to our hotel room. This hotel had room service robots that looked like dustbins with wheels. The lift door opened, and one of these robots rushed into the lift. Ladies first, said the man beside me with the accompaniment of an eyebrow dance. I grabbed my things from the room and went to meet my brother for his birthday party. We ate italian food and then went to a donut place which was apparently the only thing open this late. It was a shitty donut, and a disheveled drug addict at the front of the line was demanding something incoherent. A group of east asians behind us were striking up a conversation about who knows what with one of my brother's friends, but it was boisterous. I went back to the hotel room.

This hotel had room service robots that looked like dustbins with wheels and they made beeping sounds. The lift door opened, and one of these robots rushed into the lift. On getting off, I found myself in the top floor of the conference venue in Hilton, San Jose. I was tired. There was too much talking in this conference. I met well-known people I would have never imagined I'd ever meet, and like other people, they were people. I pitched myself and my work for the hundredth time to this man. Oh you're from CMU? Oh no I'm not. I'm not even an academic. I'm actually not even from here.

I walked down into the VIP lounge with all those famous people again. I only vaguely remember how I got access. A famous AI researcher with a thick greek accent looked at me and my shirt. Are you from Laude? Oh no I'm not. Oh your shirt made it look like that. I asked him a question about his research. I forgot his answer, it was noisy. Your shirt (a plain black shirt with a logo in the corner) is nice eh? Can I take your picture? I gave a confused nod, and he took a landscape photo of me (not a selfie) on his phone and walked off. The room was lit a shady pink, and Mr Andy (of Laude) was in the conference room yapping and having a podcast recorded. I walked to the hotel's cafe to get away from all the stimulation. I'd continue to hear an offscript podcast from him as he talked to two people a few tables away.

I saw a man eating a fries and burger in the cafe. I know he was Josh and Josh was involved in organising this conference. I waded through my fog of jet lag to meet him and said something about the conference logo. He was very excited about the logo and told me all about how it came together. I was excited too hearing about this, and now I have forgotten what he told me.

I walked out to meet an old friend, and hopped in his car. I used to worry about him because he had a negative outlook to life. I used AI to get laid, he told me. This woman was very hippie, and I learnt about birds and used that to woo her. We drove to the salt flats. The cold wind was blowing and the chilliness cut through my mental haze. I watched the california gulls flock near the deep red water. So you still talk to her? I ask. He shrugs and tells me that she ghosted him, and that she probably sensed something was off.

He drops me back, and I go through the BART in Japan town. I'm holding on to a 14kg bag and a $100 poster.

I went to an office party in SF that I was invited to. I knew no one there, except the founder from the conference booth who invited me there. I saw detroit style pizza, and a bartender who was hired for this event. An indian uncle latched on to me and started talking about his startup and his bar for talent. Another founder was next to him encouraging him to keep talking. His encouragement was unfortunately accompanied by bad breath. I was asked a question. I answered the question. The answer was dismissed and the man continued talking. I was reminded of the party that I would have in the future where people dressed as Orcs, held lightsabers to sell SaaS, and another Indian unc was selling me a database that I had no immediate use for. He was also incorrect about how that database worked.

Another person from a bigtech company struck a conversation with me. He then walked me to three women and told me what I do. All three were nodding vigorously and playacting a lot of curiosity. I awkwardly entertained this and explained what I do, and I realised that I don't actually identify myself with whatever I'm telling them.

I thanked the host for hosting me and I walked out and booked a cab to meet my brother and his wife and their friend at a bar in the corner. My $100 poster was getting dragged and pulped by the grime of san francisco.

It had been a while since I had a clear thought. I got to the airport and waited as Delta screwed up and overbooked the flights. A dad bid goodbye to their kid as they got separated. I was sat next to a person who had a recurse center tshirt. I asked him about recurse center. He had just joined Anthropic. We started talking about our respective nation's cultures while zooming in and pointing to the maps on the inflight entertainment system. We spoke for five hours straight until we landed in NYC. I took his number, so that I could tell him where to get egg shaved fuschka in Flushing, Queens, which is the best pani puri I have ever eaten. I never ate Pani Puri in NYC this time around.

entry.title: Notes from an 18-hour conversation
entry.content:
After the last Indie Web Club meet in August, we went to Tanjore as usual. From there, a few of us went to get matcha, the converstion then moved to dinner and ended only after breakfast next morning.

Here are a few notes from the conversation:

On hiring interviews, and evaluating people based on intuition

I have been doing a lot of hiring interviews lately at work. I wanted to know what criteria others have when making hiring decisions.

For me, at this point, I just want to work with people I like being around and can also have conversations with beyond work. (Which isn’t true for most people at my workplace).

The hiring interviews were for the role of Product Manager.

A majority of applicants for the role come from an engineer-turned-MBA background. A lot of these engineer-turned-MBA types are people without expertise in any specific domain. I found that they tend to rely heavily on jargon (and incredibly long monologues) to mask this lack of expertise. My experience with this tpe of Product Managers in the past have not been very pleasant either.

My colleagues’ approach to the interview was to throw random RCA (i.e. root cause analysis) questions at the candidates. Which I felt was not a very effective way to gauge anyone’s problem solving skills in a real world setting anyway.

So I’ve been relying heavily on intuition to evaluate the interviewees.

I was more interested in finding out what the person is like outside of work, and their ability to listen and have a back and forth conversation (which, sursprisingly, most candatitates were not very good at).

(In the end, the two people we hired were from unexpected backrougs. One of them had an agricultural hardware startuo and the other is a former architect, like me.)

Stop using the word art

Highly abstract words, like “art,” are a detriment to productive conversation.

The trouble with highly abstract words is that people have very different images in their minds when using the same word.

I may be thinking of the fancy editing in the last GRWM reel I saw on Instagram 2 minutes ago, while you are thinking about Michaelangelo’s frescoes in The Sistine Chapel. While both may legitimately be considered “art,” these two images are poles apart.

And while we hold these two disparate images in mind, attempts at communication will be frustrating, for we will only talk past each other.

Communication is always better when we use more specific and more sensory details to express what is on our minds. Abstraction can be a useful rhetorical tool, but in everyday conversations, it is a hindrance.

Another issue with the word “art”, in particular, is that it is used way more often to shut down conversation than to expand it. We forget that words are not real. They are merely parts of speech. In the same way a map is not the territory. But often, we treat words (like “art”) not only as real, but also sacred. Which is why critiques of a work of art is met less often with “I want to understand your perspective, why you did not like it…” (expanding the conversation) instead of “oh, but it is art!” (shutting down the conversation).

On attachment to self-identitites

We should be less attached to our self-identities.

We attach a lot of value to knowing and understanding ourselves these days. We want to know who we truly are and what our values are. Being “true to oneself,” often comes up in conversations as the destination to strive for.

It is, in some ways, misguided.

Seeking an intrinsic self-identity is paradoxical. For there is no way to express a self-identity which is not a description of the external world.

Every act of identifying oneself implies a dichotomy. I can attach my identity to, to take an example, being “kind” only if there exists an external world where there is unkindness. If I am kind, it is only relative to the world around me.

Concepts we attach to our identities to, in this way, are merely descriptions the of (i)the external world, and (ii)our relationship to the external world (i.e.: “The external world is unkind. I think I am relatively kinder than the external world. Therefore, I must be a kind person.”) They can never be truly intrinsic.

What also happens once we attach ourselves too deeply with a self-identity, is that we open ourselves to avoidable emotional strife. We get upset when our self-identities are not validated by others. (For example: I feel upset about being called unkind, because I am attached to the idea of being someone kind. I do not feel so upset about being called clumsy, for being agile is not something I am attached to.)

entry.title: Linkteresting #3: Reading, writing, webmarks, and life notes
entry.content:
Hello again webmates!

Below are some notable things I’ve read, written, and consumed lately. Click links you’re curious about—that’s what the Web is for. ☕️

Reading

  • The colors of my heart by Faiz Ahmed Faiz: A collection so good I can neither comprehend nor soak its intensity in a single reading. With revolutionary spirit, Faiz expresses discontent of both the heart and mind. His verses introspectively reflect on the innate nature of the human condition, both as individuals and as collectives. The expressions feel timeless because they are. I will have to return to the collection again for a deeper dive. P.S. The book has English translations by Baran Farooqi as well as the original poetry in Hindustani as English transliterations.
Speak, for your lips are free
Speak, for your tongue is still yours
Your upright body belongs to you
Speak, for your soul still is yours
Look, how in the blacksmith’s shop
The embers are hot, the iron glows
The mouths of the locks are being opened
Chains lengthen their reach
Speak, for the little time that you have is sufficient
Before the death of body and tongue
Speak, for the truth still lives
Speak, say all that is to be said
  • Orbital by Samantha Harvey: Her prose throughout the book is almost poetic, as remarked by Alexandra when she first suggested Orbital to me. The words are also rightfully poignant in many places. At first it seemed to me that the book has a plot but that confusingly wasn’t the case. My friend Anik, who kindly lent me the book without asking and thereby recommended it, characterized Orbital’s writing as a stream of consciousness, which is true. It took me a while to get into the groove, which is when I realized and relished its true plot: Earth itself. If you want to visualize our dazzling Earth as experienced by astronauts in dizzying pace, including what the complex maps of orbital ground tracks humanly translate into, Orbital is for you.
They look down and they understand why it’s called Mother Earth. They all feel it from time to time. They all make an association between the earth and a mother, and this in turn makes them feel like children. In their clean-shaven androgynous bobbing, their regulation shorts and spoonable food, the juice drunk through straws, the birthday bunting, the early nights, the enforced innocence of dutiful days, they all have moments up here of a sudden obliteration of their astronaut selves and a powerful sense of childhood and smallness. Their towering parent ever-present through the dome of glass.

Writing

  • Exploring the marvel that are mountains on the Moon ⛰
  • The fiery origin of our Moon tied to Earth, as unraveled by scientists through Apollo and now modern missions 🌖
A titanic collision took place 4.5 billion years ago, when the planets had just formed in a still-chaotic Solar System. A young Mars-sized planet, named Theia, slammed into the newly born Earth. The blistering impact ejected a colossal amount of material. While some of this material escaped to space, the rest stayed in orbit around Earth and coalesced to form our Moon.
  • Rocket equation 101: Revealing our Moon’s value as a launchpad
    • Poem: On the edge
  • A garden does not save the forest: Skyroot Vikram-1, the least worst case scenario for India’s launch crisis
Both for this decade and the next, India’s manifest leans squarely on the heavy-lift side in terms of mass. Even ISRO’s medium-lift PSLV rocket, with its six to seven times greater lift capacity than Vikram-1, can only cater to a smaller fraction of these mass-heavy launches. In the age of literal Moonshots and satellite constellations, the need for Vikram-1-class rockets is largely on the margins for achieving sovereign space prowess.

  • Watched Foundation. Unlike the screen adaption of amazing The Three-Body Problem novels, I did not find Foundation to be terrible. And the graphics are great, bringing some of Asimov’s ideas to the screen. It’s not a replacement for the books but a worthy watch in itself if you’re into classic Sci-Fi.
  • Calm technologies that excite me, by Abhigyan. Me too, brother.
I believe that technology should be an enabler, not a subjugator. The tinkerers that love messing with dials and diving into code should continue to do so. But otherwise, technology should help you do a thing and then stand back as you hold the reins of your human experience.
  • Refining humanity
If we thought that some activity was unique to humans, or to living beings, and we manage to get a machine to replicate that activity, we should revise our view of the activity—not our view of the machine. Creative breakthroughs in chess are not “a thing that requires a human mind,” they’re “things that can be done by human minds and by machines.”

Most of these things do not take time. Barely five minutes, or even less than that. But they need to be remembered. And several of them need to be acted upon in time in a way that you can't do anything else otherwise during then. The act of remembering and ensuring everything is executed in time seems to take up more time and bandwidth than the execution of tasks themselves.

These two days have felt more tiring than doing actual hard work of writing and publishing a long, scientific article just before. I’m aware that I’m not the only person on this planet dealing with chores in life. Many do much more every single day. My point is we have access to more and more capabilities and yet we are less and less free than ever. Most of our actions are not truly or only ours. Most of these are exactly the kind of chores that should be automated by AI, without deceit and without costing a bomb, but no, instead we want AI to write, create, and think for us. This may be the age of abundance but it’s not the age of freedom or originality.

entry.title: Even Death is a Calling
entry.content:
Through the mists and whispers of my youth, comes a calling, a calling to end it all? To die. Sounds peaceful and serene. The soft, gentle petals of the rose-colored life I envisioned, fading day by day, falling at my feet. I try to grab them, lifeless they look, all dried up and passionless. I try reaching out for other fig trees with fresh live figs, they taste sweet at first but slightly not mine, not the way I’d have tended and nurtured it. And on and on it goes, a fruitless tree, am I?

I also want to..live, the last word almost a whisper, a prayer, a begging, a permission, a last wish. As if dying were more courageous and in character than choosing to live.

I burn, I burn, I burn to live.

But what is life?

Disclaimer: The following notes deal with death in the philosophical aspect, it might have something that might make you uncomfortable, but it does not deal with any personal grief, so is safe to read.

My Notes from The Myth of Sisyphus: (till Page 52,  bf. Absurd Freedom)

The famous essay by Albert Camus, ends with quoting “One must imagine Sisyphus happy” and it annoys me. Firstly, there is the word “must”, must I imagine Sisyphus happy? It doesn’t say “can”, it doesn’t leave the possibility open. Well, it’s the concluding line, at least it concludes. I would like to reserve my opinions till the very end of reading this, as I have not read the work in toto, they will be expressed in the next post.

Camus starts his essay by talking about suicide, the reasons people commit suicide and questioning if that indeed is the right answer. He argues, dying voluntarily, means you have figured out what living requires, the effort and the uselessness of the effort. And ironically, often people who commit suicide were assured of the meaning of life. He remarks how the body came before thought and wants to live.

He insists the difference between refusing to grant meaning to life is not equivalent to suicide. He talks about how many people have thought about this and crossed the line –and given up. Camus suggests lingering longer in the deserted vegetation of our mind, for we may find some answer there.

All great deeds and all great thoughts have a ridiculous beginning. Great works are often born on a street-corner or in a restaurant’s revolving door.

In the daily humdrum of life when you suddenly pause to ask a “why”? That’s the end of your mechanical life and the birth of the Absurd. Weariness is symbolic that you are done living your automaton life and “consciousness” has taken over. Everyone lives as if not knowing death, because death is the absence of living. There are no accounts from post-dead people. They are just dead.

All human brains want to do is to unify – theories, laws, explanations – that brings them eternal joy. All existentialist philosophers agree with each other that nothing is clear, all is chaos. Knowing that the world is not reasonable but trying to unify it, because we feel the nostalgia of once being full or at home is the feeling of the Absurd. Camus exemplifies how to think of the Absurd, say a swordfighter is fighting off the machine guns. That is absurd!

Definition: the absurd does not live in the man or the world, it is the confrontation between the two. Man’s longing for comfort and meaning and the unrelentless silence of the universe.

Absurd arises from the following:
– comparison of facts and reality
– it is not inherent to either party
– it is born out of the confrontation of the facts

Camus goes on to dissect and roast Chestov and Kierkegaard, which is fun and amusing, but required me to backfill my understanding of their works. He criticizes both of them for their approach when they were finally face to face with the Absurd. According to Camus, Chestov’s approach was to start hoping beyond the Absurd and Kierkegaard attributed it to religiousness, and that Christianity will explain the absurd. Kierkegaard wants to be cured of his nostalgia. (My notes say: “yeah, I don’t blame him”)

When Chestov can’t find answers to the unreasonable, he deifies it as God and admits there is no justification for it. The gap he feels is the bedrock of transcendence. Camus call this a leap.

Camus claims that by making absurd as part of the universe, Chestov eludes the problem of having to face it.

Kierkegaard bows down to Christianity when faced with the Absurd. Camus calls this also a leap.

And this is attitude, this leaping to explain the Absurd by attributing it to God or God-like properties, is what he calls “Philosophical Suicide”.

He then began countering Husserl, the last contender but the most respected, he goes till the very end, the theory of reality being by fragmented projections of the actual experience, we cannot explain it but only describe it. Camus counters this with Husserl bringing heaven to earth, every moment is privileged, there is God in every atom of the human soul, immanence instead of transcendence.

 

Quotes from the book:

These scents of grass and stars at night, certain evenings when the heart relaxes—how shall I negate this world whose power and strength I feel? Yet all the knowledge on earth will give me nothing to assure me that this world is mine.

Heidegger considers the human condition coldly and announces that that existence is humiliated. The only reality is “anxiety” in the whole chain of beings.

entry.title: The fiery origin of our Moon tied to Earth, as unraveled by scientists through Apollo and now modern missions
entry.content:
Where did our Moon come from? The origin of Earth’s cosmic companion is a fundamental question in planetary science. From Galileo’s first telescopic observations of the Moon to humans walking on its surface, our understanding of its origins has come a long way. Yet it’s far from complete.

Over the decades, scientists have proposed multiple hypotheses to attempt explaining how the Moon came to be. In this article, I focus on the one with the highest consensus among scientists: the Giant Impact Hypothesis (GIH). According to the GIH, a titanic collision took place 4.5 billion years ago, when the planets had just formed in a still-chaotic Solar System. A young Mars-sized planet, named Theia, slammed into the newly born Earth. The blistering impact ejected a colossal amount of material. While some of this material escaped to space, the rest stayed in orbit around Earth and coalesced to form our Moon.

The best evidences for the GIH come from NASA’s Apollo Moon landings between 1969 and 1972, whose 382 kilograms of lunar rock, soil, and core samples brought to Earth allowed us to test multiple hypotheses in various ways. 300 grams of samples fetched by the former Soviet Union’s three Luna missions also contributed to our understanding. The picture of the Moon’s formation emerging from Apollo and Luna sample studies has been anything but simple. The results have been difficult to reconcile and interpret for scientists. Here’s a rundown of some key findings, both for and against the GIH.

Findings in support of the GIH

Magma ocean

The GIH implies that the newly formed Moon post-Earth-impact must be in a molten state. Scientists have estimated our Moon to have been covered in a vast magma ocean at least 500 kilometers deep. Over time, this magma would crystallize to form the Moon’s mantle and crust. During this process, heavier minerals like olivine and pyroxene would’ve sunk to form the mantle. And lower density minerals, principally plagioclase, would float on top and crystallize into light anorthosite-based crust, which is what the bright “highland” regions on the Moon we see should be made of.

The GIH further predicts that during this process, any chemically incompatible elements in the magma would get sandwiched between the crust and mantle, forming what is known as KREEP-rich magma. KREEP is an acronym built from the letters K (Potassium), REE (rare-earth elements) and P (Phosphorus). The REE part encompasses heat-producing and radioactive elements such as thorium.

The very first lunar samples, brought to Earth by Apollo 11 contained millimetric fragments from the rocky highlands nearby. These fragments were not only found to be made of anorthosites but had KREEP-rich materials as well, suggesting a molten state for the ancient Moon and supporting the GIH. Samples from later Apollo missions and Luna ones supported the hypothesis too.

The lunar core

Also supporting the GIH were three independent experiments on Apollo missions that provided scientists insights into the Moon’s interior. Data from the Passive Seismic Experiments, Laser Ranging Retroreflectors, and Lunar Surface Magnetometers all implied that the Moon’s core shouldn’t be larger than 900 kilometers. That means the lunar core, solid and liquid combined, represents only about 25 percent of the Moon’s radius, in contrast to about 50 percent for other rocky planets like Earth. The GIH predicts that the Earth-Theia collision would result in Theia’s core getting absorbed into Earth, leaving a smaller core mass for the Moon. The calculated sizes of the Moon’s core from these three independent experiments thus agrees with the GIH. It’s also worth noting that Earth is the densest planet in our Solar System, which could be explained by the absorption of Theia’s core.

Volatile depletion

Another area of interest for the GIH is volatiles, which are elements with low boiling points such as nitrogen, water, carbon dioxide, hydrogen and more. Their low boiling points mean their abundances on planetary bodies deplete with time, inversely proportional to factors like the object’s gravity. On the Moon, large scale volatile depletion could’ve been due to two processes happening at different times: first, the evaporation of volatiles when the Moon formed and second, evaporation from ancient volcanism.

Scientists figured that studying isotopes—which are different subatomic forms of a given element—in existing lunar volatiles will help us know the Moon’s past. Since isotopes in volatiles deplete differently based on the nature of the event, the kinds we measure can tell us which and how much of the above two processes shaped the Moon of today. For example, lighter isotopes of Zinc would get evaporated in large amounts during the Moon’s fiery formation but remain unaffected by volcanic processes.

Scientists observed in Apollo samples that lighter isotopes of Zinc are less abundant than the heavier ones. This means large amounts of volatiles were indeed lost during the Moon’s formation, supporting the GIH prediction of a fiery formation of Luna from a volatile-rich Earth.

Findings against the GIH

Titanium isotopes

If the Moon indeed formed from the collision of two objects as the GIH posits, it should’ve inherited some of its material from Earth and some from Theia. One way to test that is to measure the titanium isotopic composition of the Moon and compare it to Earth’s. If the Moon formed from both Earth’s and Theia’s materials, its titanium signature should be a mix of both. Titanium is a good element to measure because it isn’t easily vaporized and tends to remain solid or molten even at high temperatures. Our Moon’s titanium abundances should thus roughly be in the same state now as during its formation.

Comparative analysis of titanium in Apollo samples indicates that the Moon’s titanium came from Earth alone; it’s not a mix of Earth and Theia. In stark contrast, meteorites found on Earth show two orders of magnitude larger variations in titanium isotopes, indicating their distinct and varied origins. How then could the GIH be correct?

One unlikely explanation is that Theia had the same composition as Earth but that’s a long shot. Computer simulations of the GIH collision by Caltech researchers in 2007 estimated the origin of various materials relative to the Sun, and how they would’ve been distributed across the early Solar System. They found the likelihood of Theia naturally having an identical isotopic composition to Earth to be less than 1%. And so for the Moon to have identical titanium signatures as the Earth is a major anomaly for the GIH. Many scientists call it the “isotope crisis”.

On the other hand, scientists proposed in 2021 that the two continent-sized regions discovered in Earth’s mantle with greater density, one beneath Africa and one beneath the Pacific Ocean, could be Theia’s remains. That between Earth and the Moon, the former would’ve absorbed most of Theia’s material not lost to space. In 2022, scientists published a study of six lunar meteorites, which concluded that the Moon’s noble gases like helium and neon come from Earth too, bolstering the GIH.

A shared water source for Earth and Luna

Much like the case with titanium, the isotopic compositions of lunar hydrogen and oxygen can be compared with that of Earth. The volcanic glass samples brought back from Apollo 15 and 17 had minor quantities of water in them. The isotopic composition of hydrogen in this water is nearly identical to that of water in Earth’s mantle. Likewise, the Moon’s oxygen isotopic composition, measured in Apollo 11, 12, 15, 16 and 17 samples, also show identical natures to Earth. When compared to other Solar System objects, such as Mars, the Earth-Moon system is thus compositionally distinct from them and identical to each other, with seemingly no trace of a distinct Theia in Luna. More recent and higher precision data suggests a slight difference in oxygen isotopes between Earth and the Moon, suggesting Theia’s presence albeit only minimally.

Iron isotopes of the Earth and Moon are identical too. Some of the latest measurements (open access) of iron composition and distribution in lunar samples, Earth rocks, and meteorites entrench the outcome but do suggest a slight variation possibility between Terra and Luna from a Theia formed closer to the Sun than Earth.

In any case, the Earth-Moon isotope crisis remains across all modern measurements at large across titanium, oxygen, iron, and so on. In oxygen’s case especially though, a much broader study is necessary because Apollo landing sites represent a small slice of the Moon’s diversity, all being near-equatorial and on the nearside. When scientists study lunar water ice and oxygen-rich polar soil samples fetched by future missions, and determine the relative contributions of various sources of the Moon’s water and oxygen, it will provide us a far firmer basis for any comparative analysis on the origins of Earth and Luna.

Chang’e and Chandrayaan contribute

Some modern missions have continued contributing to the endeavor of figuring out the specifics of our Moon and Earth’s origin story.

With robotic instruments for surface-only studies becoming increasingly advanced, scientists suggested in 2021 that even non-sample-return missions can now provide some significant insights with higher precision measurements that before, especially if performed in key and diverse places on the Moon. India’s Chandrayaan 3 mission falls in that category. It landed on the Moon’s nearside in August 2023 at the near-polar location of 69.37°S, 32.32°E, which lies far away from Apollo and Luna sampling sites. The Chandrayaan 3 rover Pragyan made lunar soil composition measurements using its X-ray spectrometer, finding it broadly similar to Apollo and Luna samples. This bolstered our Moon’s fully molten origin scenario as laid out by the GIH, or extended its validity to high-latitude regions on the nearside at the very least.

The fact that the elemental measurements came from a unique region on the Moon is important. Factions of scientists have been counter-hypothesizing that our Moon was either only partially molten (PDF) after its formation or that the lunar crust didn’t solidify homogeneously enough (PDF), both tenets opposing the GIH’s dominant global magma ocean model. Chandrayaan 3’s measured compositional ground truth thus uniquely casted a metaphorical wide net across the Moon. There’s also a small chance the rover might have stumbled upon lunar mantle material amid measurements of volatiles. Its detection of such materials makes the Chandrayaan 3 landing region a potential mantle sampling location for future missions and studies of the Moon and Earth’s origins. From the paper:

Prior to ISRO’s Chandrayaan-3 mission, there were no in-situ volatile abundance measurements from the lunar southern high-latitude highlands. Consequently, our understanding of the variations in the concentrations of volatiles across the lunar surface is constrained by the limited scope of measurements obtained primarily from lunar samples collected from equatorial regions. This points to a substantial gap in our understanding of the mechanisms governing enrichment-depletion of volatiles such as sodium (Na), potassium (K) and sulfur (S) on the Moon.

Of course, more grounded and more versatile studies still require and benefit from samples. In 2024, China’s Chang’e 6 spacecraft collected samples from the Moon’s farside, a world first. Since then, fervent studies of the samples have transformed our understanding of the Moon’s evolution by anchoring key events in the lunar timeline. In one such study, Chinese researchers analyzed two grams of Chang’e 6 samples and found the isotopic measurements of key chemical elements to be compatible with a fully molten young Moon. Chang’e 6 thus lent unequivocal credence to the GIH, anchoring a key event in our Moon’s origin and evolution.

Another Chang’e 6 study analyzing 578 particles revealed for the first time that the Moon’s farside mantle contains less water than within the nearside, another factor in the contrasting farside-nearside volcanic activity. The finding added to the debate on the topic in a grounded and unique way, favoring the GIH hypothesis that our Moon indeed lost a major portion of its water and its constituents amid a fiery formation.

Future findings

While various forms of modifications of the GIH have been proposed to account for deviances in evidences, the fact remains that specifics of the Moon’s and Earth’s origin stories are still a mystery. Despite the fact that Apollo missions landed in largely similar geological areas, they still transformed our understanding of the Moon’s possible origins. At the same time, its results left us with more knowledge but farther away from a firm conclusion, a common outcome in complex scientific research. Chandrayaan and Chang’e results added nuanced layers to our understanding gained from Apollo while opening new questions still.

To continue piecing together the complex origin and history of the Earth-Moon system, we need samples from new locations, including geologically pristine rocks below the lunar surface, the poles, and the farside. We need to probe the nature of water on the Moon’s poles and in the lunar interior to know their origins. A nice, detailed review paper, Origin of the Moon, summarizes recent advances in our knowledge. The paper highlights ten key datasets that would clear the dust on our Moon’s formation. This includes getting a better understanding of the role of magnetic fields, which likely accelerated the process. An intriguing inclusion in the list is measuring the isotopic composition of Venus so that scientists can get a better grip on what made the inner solar nebula, and thus Theia and early Earth. Upcoming missions to Venus from India, Europe, and the US could provide anchor points to that end. Researchers are also bringing advanced simulations to the field, overcoming limitations of past computational models and better analyzing possible compositions of Earth, Theia, and Luna. This will help researchers determine specific measurements future missions can make to help us know if our Moon has a blue origin.

Later this decade or early next, India’s Chandrayaan 4 & Chandrayaan 5 spacecraft as well as multiple crewed missions from China and the US’ Artemis program aim to explore south polar sites. The region is intertwined scientifically to the Moon’s internal structure and thus its formation and evolution. The poles are also where water ice and other volatiles persist, allowing scientists to close in on the goal. Other than on-ground measurements by such missions and its findings, there will be detailed studies of samples brought by Chinese and US crewed flights as well as India’s robotic Chandrayaan 4. These samples are expected to host pieces of ancient crustal and potential mantle materials. Crewed missions in particular are expected to bring more diverse and more amount of samples over time. Much like Apollo, studying a fresh set of novel samples will likely transform not just how we look at our Moon and Earth but also the Solar System and beyond. Luna’s pristine interior compared to other geologically active worlds means it helps researchers understand the baseline layer of processes that drive the interior evolution of rocky worlds everywhere.

What a profound success it would be to unravel the origin story of our dear Moon and Earth. Being the most accessible and well preserved body in our Solar System to study fundamental planetary processes, our Moon beckons. 🌖

I don’t use AI to write a single word and cite everything.

entry.title: Midjourneying through rural Indonesia
entry.content:
This post started off as a talk proposal last year. It didn't end up getting selected. I recently found it in my drafts and decided to build on it and write about my Midjourney experiments from 2025.

Jiva.ag was an Agritech startup operating in Indonesia. Our operations spanned the entire agricultural ecosystem—we extended credit to farmers, purchased their harvests, supplied agro-retailers, and even sold our own white-labeled agricultural products.

We weren't just a tech company but one where our business required a strong physical presence on the ground. We regularly held activation events in small towns and villages (even sponsored a football team) which needed a steady stream of visual marketing materials. In the early days, the product design team pitched in to support marketing with everything from logo creation and Figma templates to t-shirt designs. Eventually we invested into creating a small, in-house Brand design team.

Filling a representation gap

One of the first goals of the Brand design team was to come up with a new visual language. The original Jiva visual language had started to feel dated, and with our growing focus on agro-retailing, we needed a much brighter, more vibrant market presence.

As part of this initiative, the team decided to anchor our new marketing collaterals around a heavily photograph-centric approach. However this created a new problem. Over the years, we had regularly invested in capturing film and photography content on the ground but this approach required us to have a lot of images to work with. To make matters worse, the stock photo libraries we subscribed to were lacking when it came to representation of rural Indonesian folk.

Getting a Midjourney Pro account, helped fill this gap. The team didn't need to wait for an on-ground team to go out on the field for creating assets for use. They could just generate them, or create variations of existing ones with little effort leading to short turnaround times.

Speeding up a feature

Around the same time, Juneza was working with the retailers and noticed an un-met user need. Our retailers needed help marketing their store and with liquidating their stock. Solving this problem was important to us as we were about to launch our own Agri-brand; Jivaprodi.

Juneza's research had uncovered that the larger retailers did leverage digital marketing. Some of them used Instagram/Whatsapp to post Farmer testimonials while others advertized loyalty programs using Canva templates.

The business stakeholders felt that this was something we should be pursuing so a scrappy team of three; me, Kesha and Sivan, decided to take it up as a side project. For the MVP, I made a few mockups in Figma for leadership alignment and I started working on how AI Image generation would fit into this feature.

It was Ramadan, and Lebaran—the celebration marking the end of Ramadan, also known as Eid al-Fitr—was just a couple of weeks away. The entire country effectively slows down for the Lebaran holidays as people travel back to their often remote hometowns to be with their families.

For farmers, the timing was particularly relevant. Many would sell their harvest in the lead-up to this period, so they would have money to spend during Lebaran. It felt like the right moment to launch something that could help retailers remain top of mind with their customers.

Ofcourse there was not enough time. Back then, image generation was still early. We had just got AI to generate the right number of human appendages. But the tech was still too hallucinatory at that point (and still is) and it wasn't able to generate text either. We did not want any controversy so instead we went ahead with generating and curating the posters. In the end, we finalized six Ramadan greetings and three promotional posters.. The customization in this iteration was minimal. I made the posters using Figma and Canva and instead of getting user input, we decided to go and add the name and number from our system directly.

Impact

We launched it right before the Lebaran week with a small marketing campaign. We even made a short video introducing the tool voiced by Kesha. And over the next few weeks, we saw that the users who used it kept coming back to share more. Every month we created and added more topical posters to the repo (with Fafa’s help).

In just under 3 weeks, we were able to ship this feature out from design to development and 10% of our active users ended up sharing posters in that 1 week. This wouldnt have been possible without having access to generative AI imagery.

Extending a design team's production capacity

I moved my focus to Jiva Lite, the new initiative that we had started working on (You can read about it here). Jiva Lite was our attempt to simplify the crop procurement process via WhatsApp chat. It was designed to be lightweight and aimed to attract users primarily through digital channels.

As part of that initiative, we designed websites, created onboarding videos and ofcourse ran ad campaigns. Facebook (meta) became a primary channel to deliver ads and during this process, I learnt that Facebook's ads come with an expiry date. Over a few weeks, every asset eventually reduces in terms of CTR and needs to be refreshed periodically. Sometimes it's obvious what works and other times, it isn't. We didn't have the design bandwidth to enable that constant creation and exploration. The brand design team was busy with the offline brand marketing collaterals and couldn't help us. So I decided to leverage Midjourney to create assets and use the newly released 'animate' feature to explore video ad creation. I assembled the final ad in Figma(image) or by using Instagram Story creator(video).

I know it's hard to believe now but I was a AI skeptic back then. I was reluctant to use AI but these projects showed me the potential of the technology. It amplified our small design team at Jiva and enabled us to explore, experiment and deliver at a level that was not possible before.

Today, I'm no longer a skeptic and use AI to bring my silly ideas into reality. But it's not just that, we've seen AI helping people to find solutions to rare diseases, save languages from extinction and even attempt to identify patterns in animal communication. Yes, there is a lot of uncertainity about the tech, and I do agree that there aren't enough safeguards or regulations in place. But never before has cutting edge tech been available at this scale to the general public and at such a subsidized price point.

It's truly a strange, uncertain and genuinely interesting time to be alive.

entry.title: Weeknote 35 2026
entry.content:
Welcome back to another late weeknote 🥲. I was initially just gonna say: "I was busy this weekend too", but I wanted to understand what was it that actually stopped me from publishing this weeknote on time. I usually write weeknotes on Sunday mornings, and for the last three weeks, I genuinely have been busy during that time. First was shifting houses, second was a trip where I didn't even have my laptop with me, and the third and the latest is because I was out climbing on real rocks in Raogudlu. But well, details about that will be revealed in next weeknote xD.

Life

Poem

I published a poem this week! I wrote it while enjoying a magnificent sunset upon a small lake. Gazing at the reflection of mountains in the lake, a stroke of inspiration hit and the poem was ready half an hour later :). This poem is aimed at people who are just tagging along in life, flowing wherever it takes, no struggles, no ambitions, just existing. This is a plea to them to struggle (tatake)! Have something you can struggle for! You will enjoy your lives so much more.

Concert

I attended The Yellow Diary's concert this Saturday, it was SO MAGICAL! This was my first ever concert and I am so happy it was this!!! I have been listening to their songs for a very long time but mostly consuming them passively. Never realizing a bunch of separate songs I have been savouring, were from this single band. I had so many OH moments over the last two weeks, slowly realizing so many songs from my playlist were from them 😭.

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/479gm_eecJ4?si=jX3UkkIZDIL9iBJz

P.S. ignore the guy singing right into my phone 😭

Hangouts

One of my motivations of moving near to my climbing gym was spending more time with my climbing friends. I was not a big fan of paying for cabs every other night and hence often skipped group hangout plans. But now, now is different. I live in walking/cycling distances from everyone and would love to hang out with them more! This Thursday one such impromptu plan happened, but I am not sure I want more of these, we were up till 3:30 AM in the night playing Contact! We literally made sure we had covered each and every letter from A-Z. Only thing fueling us was Chai shots at a random shop whose owner's only entertainment was looking at us shouting Contact randomly followed by spewing words all of us had forgotten for years. Resultantly, Contact has been banned in our group for a few months 😂. But it was fun, maybe maybe again sometime :P.

Break pads

I decided to get my cycle's break pads changed for extra safety and peace of mind. I started looking for a repair place and spent a bunch of time trying to find a cheap one at that in Indiranagar itself. Sadly, there's no good advice online! All of them point to the expensive stores where I would need to spend my cycle's worth just to step in. But a random query at a car garage store sent me down a rabbit hole of finding this small shop near Bob's bar. It turned out to be pretty nearby to my house and I got pads replaced plus air check plus brake alignment correction, all for 90 rupees only! FAFO wins :).

Acidity

I prefer eating less spiced (masaledar) food in general and also having just one chai in a day. Both of these things have gone haywire ever since I shifted here. This would not have been a problem unless I found myself having acidity suddenly. I am now on a hunt for what exactly is causing this. Divide and conquer, first suspect is chai, second is the extra spice I am consuming in food here.

Climbing

This week I didn't spend a lot of time climbing, but the limited time spent was super high quality one! On Tuesday, I again spent my session working on the overhang level 5. This time it was with my usual climbing gang and OH BOY they helped me so much! I had a completely different beta by the end of the session and was reasonably confident that I can get it in the next one!!

And on Thursday, finally after four sessions spanning 4-5 hours each...I SENT IT!! YESSS!!!!! I am screaming writing this weeknote, I am so happy I can cry. This is definitely not a level 5, so many of my strong friends couldn't even make the start move, and to make it worse, start is not even the crux move 🫠. Every move can be refined with careful body positioning and micro-betas. All of the hard work came together in the end, and I was at the top, matching the final hold. I was also lucky enough to get the exact send in video! Angle got a bit weird, and one might not be able to assess how hard the start is, but I don't care, this weeknote is the evidence and memoir for that!

https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/x4_JKFWuEj0?mute=1

Thursday was actually a very good day, except this level 5, in the new set I did everything from level 1 to level 5 and also got a level 6!! All on the same day! Some days you die of thirst, meanwhile on some you are drowning in success! What a week, I am satisfied. Now time to project even harder purple level 5 in the cave. It has such a bad one arm lockoff, I had to make sure my bicep got enough rest for a week!

Swimming

I went to tryout Game Theory's swimming pool in Ulsoor. They charged me 370 for an hour!! For a reminder, I used to pay 70 rupees for an hour in Jayanagar! What a ripoff. They even had a weird situation where people were learning swimming, doing laps and training scuba diving, all in one single pool. 😭

I am absolutely not happy with the swimming pool situation here, but sadly this is the best pool around 🥲. Maybe when I return, I will take a membership here, with membership it becomes cheaper but not as cheap as Jayanagar. Well you gain some, you lose some....

Food

  • I tried Subway Paneer Loaded Sandwhich, it was ehh, not ordering it again. Free chocolate cookie was tasty tho 😋.
  • I also tried a bunch of local bakeries in Kerala! It was a feast of cream buns, carrot and plum cakes, some rice and jaggery sweet, small sweetend breads, and so much more I don't know names of/can't describe!!
  • There will be a bunch of different places listed in my in progress trip blog :).

Work

We made amazing progress on integration of logical table readers integration.

  • Iceberg with immediate consistency is blazingly fast when compared to our old stack. ⚡ Surprising thing is we did these benchmarks with immediate consistency ON on our new stack and OFF on our old stack (read without and with caching respectively).
  • We also merged support for Delta and plan parquet tables. Both of them are strictly on par/better when compared to old stack, again with immediate consistency ON in new stack and OFF in old one!

Tech

I have developed a sudden interest in k8s and its internal operations. I have been brushing up again how k8s works, but this time not just covering its objects, but how does it work on the fundamental level! I have spent so much time understanding, how Service are just VIP and they only exist in ip routing table of the nodes. How CNI, CSI, CRI works. How external load balancers are integrated with details covering L2 routing, BGP routing and external load balancers of AWS! Expect few blog posts around the same soon!

TV Show

It was a surprisingly low watchtime week. Last week I was watched till episode 10, but this week I didn't even complete one episode. Episode 11 is still in progress, damn that was a busy week!

Reads

For many years, I've regarded compiler construction as one of the most  
scientific, disciplined, and algorithmic areas of computer science. There is  
something wonderfully satisfying about a field in which so much can be derived  
systematically rather than done by the seat of the pants.  
  
The difficulty, at least in my experience, is that there simply aren't that  
many jobs writing compilers. Occasionally I get a small job writing a  
dedicated parser, but for the most part I have little opportunity to use  
compiler algorithms professionally. That makes it hard to justify spending my  
limited time keeping those skills fresh.  
  
And now I wonder whether LLMs will reduce the demand for some kinds of  
compiler and parser expertise even further.  
  
So I'm curious what people on this list think: **Why should a computer science  
student today take a compiler course?**  
  
Do students take compiler courses because the techniques they learn are likely  
to be useful in their careers, despite the relatively small number of jobs  
involving compiler development? Or is the real value of a compiler course that  
it teaches broader ways of thinking about languages, grammars,  
representations, transformations, optimization, and software systems?  
  
And has the arrival of LLMs changed your answer at all?

I really liked this answer from a mathematician on it:

As a mathematician, I can only comment on this as an outsider. But perhaps an  
outside perspective has some value here.  
  
Even though in mathematics (to my regret) it has become increasingly common to  
motivate topics by explaining what they might be useful for later, most of  
what we teach is about things that already exist. We teach theorems that have  
already been proved. Exercises and exam questions have usually been asked  
before in similar, and sometimes even identical, form.  
  
Since the arrival of LLMs, there has been something close to panic among some  
colleagues that students can now simply solve everything with ChatGPT. What  
tends to be forgotten is that students could always copy solutions to homework  
or take-home exams from other students without understanding them. They could  
also memorize solutions to standard exam problems without understanding why  
they work.  
  
But there have also always been students who wanted to know _why_  something  
works, either because they were curious from the beginning or because somebody  
managed to make them curious. They wanted to understand how one might come up  
with a proof rather than merely reproduce it. Those students gradually  
developed their own ways of thinking. Later they were not only better at  
dealing with known theorems and standard problems, but also at developing  
creative ideas when confronted with problems they had never seen before.  
  
Mathematics has done rather well with the idea that learning how existing  
things work prepares you for challenges you do not yet know. That also means  
not merely using tools — known theorems, for example — without having any idea  
why they work.  
  
Of course it is neither possible nor necessary to understand everything down  
to the last detail. But I think it helps enormously to enjoy trying to  
understand as much as possible, without constantly being distracted by the  
question “what will this be useful for?” If you really understand something,  
some useful consequence will often turn out to be a by-product — possibly one  
that nobody could have predicted when you learned it.  
  
I have no idea which problems LLMs (which I use myself) will be able to solve  
better than I can in the future. But I suspect I will be able to use them much  
better if I understand which problems I can delegate to them as part of  
solving a larger problem that they cannot yet solve the way I can.  
  
And coming back to compilers: I find it difficult to understand why one would  
_not_  want to know how a compiler works. Quite apart from whether one will  
ever write a compiler professionally, I think it is simply interesting to  
understand how the thing that turns your program into something a machine can  
execute actually works.  
  
  
Michael Lehn  
  
University of Ulm, Institute for Numerical Mathematics  
Helmholtzstr. 20  
D-89069 Ulm, Germany

entry.title: How much gamedev can you learn before GTA 6 launches day 2!
entry.content:
Check out Mogura Smash

Fixing bugs

So last time i mentioned that there was a bug. Basically my characters animation was not running in the web build which I had exported.

But for some reason it was working on my machine!

Instead of fixing the issue I spent some time prioritizing finshing up the animations for the walk cycle.

Not really a painstaking process, infact pixel art is quite zen.

That being said the art is still sort of placeholder at the moment. I am trying to kill my inner perfectionist and instead focusing on building something crappy and getting it all out the door, it is practice after all.

So after finishing up the walking animation and writing the code needed to get the correct animation playing I can confidently say that I am able to implement 2d animations in Godot!!!

In the end the bug fix was pretty simple, usually when the feature is broken in prod but not in dev, I make it a point to check the build pipeline. That's where something usually goes wrong in my limited experience and turns out I was right. My github action was using an older version of godot and I needed to update it to the one I was using in my machine.

Primary Gameplay loop

I think I have watched enough devlogs on youtube to know that it is very easy to make good looking visuals for a game, but have nothing interesting in the way of gameplay. That is where the primary gameplay loop comes into picture.

A primary gameplay loop is defined as what the player will be doing moment to moment while playing the game. If you want to distill it down it is meaningful actions and decisions that a player can make when presented with a challenge or scenario such that they are able to make some kind of impact on the playable state getting some feedback or reward and the cycle goes on.

In Super Mario Bros, the primary gameplay loop revolves around moving from left to right and having the option of jumping on top of enemies to take them out of the play space,or dodging them. You have the option of using the powerups as well and they make a meningful impact on how you engage for example if you have a fire flower.

Another example is the 30 seconds of fun from Halo, where the designers made Halo in such a way that they were able to make a series of these 30 seconds of fun into a pretty cool trilogy and prequel.

Yahtzee Crowshaw who is my favorite game critic drilled this into my head, and when I am making up games in my head this is usually where the fantasy of making a game meets the reality of designing a game. I am usually stuck in the process of these elaboirate imaginary games with rich epic stories and when i actually sit down and think about what the player is actually doing I have diddly.

So for my game Mogura Smash I am thinking of something simple like a survivor lite or just a whack a mole thing. It is not going to be the only thing I will be making in the duration of this challenge so it doesn't make sense to put all my eggs in one basket. So just Rip it and Ship It.
